items.headline: Can Stem Cell Therapy in Thailand Offer Hope for Australian Diabetes Patients?
items.preview: Stem cell therapy in Thailand presents a promising option for Australian diabetes patients, focusing on pancreatic regeneration.
items.article:
Stem cell therapy for diabetes in Thailand offers Australian patients a promising pathway to advanced treatment, focusing on regenerating damaged pancreatic cells and improving insulin function. This innovative approach can lead to significant improvements in glycemic control and reduced medication dependence.
Why this matters: Patients often experience cost savings of 50-70% compared to treatments in Australia, making specialized care more accessible. Thailand has emerged as a prominent destination for medical tourism, renowned for its cutting-edge facilities and highly skilled medical professionals.
The therapy targets the root causes of diabetes by repairing damaged insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Evidence suggests that many patients experience improved glycemic control and can decrease their reliance on insulin or oral medications. The findings highlight the potential of stem cell therapy as a game-changer in diabetes management for Australians seeking advanced care abroad.

items.headline: Bryan Johnson’s chronic disease is notoriously difficult to diagnose
items.preview: Bryan Johnson reveals his struggle with autoimmune gastritis, a challenging condition to diagnose.
items.article:
Longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson shared some bad news on social media recently, stating, 'I have an autoimmune disease. My stomach is eating itself.' The disease, autoimmune gastritis, is a chronic inflammatory condition that can lead to serious complications like stomach cancer.
Why this matters: Autoimmune gastritis affects an estimated 4% of people worldwide but is often misdiagnosed. Johnson's case highlights the need for increased awareness and better diagnostic practices among gastroenterologists. Experts suggest that more biopsies should be performed on patients with a history of iron deficiency to identify this condition early.
Johnson's announcement serves as a reminder that despite efforts to optimize health, diseases can still arise, underscoring the importance of regular screenings and awareness of symptoms related to chronic conditions.

items.headline: Long-Term Stem Cell Data Boosts Chronic Stroke Recovery Research
items.preview: New data on iPSC-derived neural progenitor cells shows promise for chronic stroke recovery.
items.article:
In a breakthrough presentation at the ISSCR 2026 Annual Meeting, researchers disclosed long-term clinical data on hNPC01, an iPSC-derived neural progenitor cell therapy for chronic ischemic stroke. This Phase I study provides compelling evidence on the safety and biological activity of this novel regenerative approach.
Why this matters: Stroke is a leading cause of disability, and current rehabilitation strategies often plateau after the chronic phase. The hNPC01 therapy aims to replace lost neurons and repair damaged brain circuits, offering hope for patients with persistent motor disabilities.
The study revealed that transplanted cells can survive over extended periods and potentially contribute to functional improvements. These findings mark a crucial milestone in translating regenerative neuroscience into clinical practice, paving the way for larger studies to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of neural progenitor transplantation.

items.headline: Roche drops two Huntington’s programmes from Ionis
items.preview: Roche discontinues two Huntington's disease programs after disappointing trial results.
items.article:
Roche has discontinued two Huntington’s disease programmes after its Ionis-partnered drug tominersen failed to improve patients’ symptoms. This decision eliminates two of Roche’s three clinical approaches to lowering the toxic huntingtin protein associated with the disease.
Why this matters: The phase 2 GENERATION HD2 trial found that while tominersen reduced mutant huntingtin levels, it had no meaningful effect on clinical outcomes, prompting Roche to end the programme. The company is now left with only one remaining clinical programme for Huntington’s disease, which highlights the challenges in developing effective treatments for this condition.
Roche's decision reflects the ongoing difficulties in finding disease-modifying therapies for Huntington’s disease, a condition for which no approved treatments currently exist.

items.headline: GABA neurons in the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus suppress wakefulness in healthy and narcoleptic mice
items.preview: Research identifies GABA neurons as key regulators of wakefulness and potential narcolepsy targets.
items.article:
Recent findings reveal that GABAergic neurons in the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD) suppress wakefulness in both healthy and narcoleptic mice. This study utilized optogenetics to demonstrate that silencing these neurons induces robust wakefulness, while their activation promotes NREM sleep.
Why this matters: Understanding the role of SLDGABA neurons could lead to new therapeutic targets for narcolepsy, a disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep attacks. The research suggests that these neurons play a critical role in regulating arousal state transitions, highlighting their potential as intervention targets for narcolepsy treatment.
The findings not only clarify the function of SLDGABA neurons but also open avenues for developing treatments aimed at managing narcolepsy symptoms more effectively.
